question: Why does nums = nums.sort() lead to the error 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'append'?
answer: nums = nums.sort() leads to the error 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'append' because list.sort() sorts the list in place and returns None. [S1] To avoid this error, use nums.sort() on its own line or use sorted(nums) to get a new sorted list [S1].

3. Lookup Errors Compared
KeyError is raised when a dictionary key is missing. IndexError is raised when a sequence index is
out of range. AttributeError is raised when an object has no attribute of that name.
The message 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'append' almost always means a variable holds
None instead of a list. The classic cause is writing nums = nums.sort(), because list.sort() sorts in
place and returns None. Use nums.sort() on its own line or sorted(nums) when a new list is
needed.
dict.get(key, default) avoids a KeyError, while collections.defaultdict(list) creates a missing key with
an empty list the first time it is accessed, which makes grouping code shorter.

S2.title: Python Reference Notes
S2.text:
BUILT-IN FUNCTIONS
len(x) returns the number of items in x.
sum(nums) adds the numbers in an iterable.
min(nums) and max(nums) return the smallest and largest items.
sorted(items) returns a new sorted list; list.sort() sorts in place and returns None.
enumerate(items) gives (index, item) pairs.
zip(a, b) pairs items from two iterables and stops at the shortest.
range(stop) generates 0 .. stop-1; range(start, stop, step) supports steps.
isinstance(x, int) tests whether x is an instance of a type.

S3.title: Python Lecture Notes
S3.text: 4. Lists, Tuples, Sets and Dictionaries A list is an ordered, mutable sequence: nums = [3, 1, 2]. Common methods are append(x) to add at the end, insert(i, x), remove(x), pop() to remove and return the last item, and sort() to sort in place. The built-in sorted(nums) returns a new sorted list and leaves the original unchanged. List comprehensions build lists concisely: [n * n for n in nums if n > 1]. A tuple is an ordered but immutable sequence, written (1, 2). Tuples are used for fixed records and can be dictionary keys because they are hashable. A set stores unique, unordered elements and supports fast membership tests plus union (|), intersection (&) and difference (-). A dictionary maps keys to values: ages = {"Ali": 20, "Mona": 22}. S4.title: Python Lecture Notes
S4.text: 1. Variables and Data Types A variable is a name that refers to a value stored in memory. In Python you create a variable by assignment, for example age = 21. Python is dynamically typed: the type belongs to the value, not to the name, so the same name can later refer to a string. The core built-in types are int (whole numbers), float (decimal numbers), str (text), bool (True or False) and NoneType (the single value None, meaning "no value"). The function type(x) reports the type of x. Conversion functions such as int("42"), float("3.5") and str(10) create new values of another type; int("abc") raises a ValueError. Strings are immutable sequences of characters. Indexing starts at zero, so "python"[0] is "p", and negative indexes count from the end, so "python"[-1] is "n". Slicing "python"[1:4] returns "yth" (start included, stop excluded).

S5.title: Python Lecture Notes
S5.text: 6. Object-Oriented Programming A class is a blueprint and an object is an instance of that class. The special method __init__ initializes a new object, and self is the conventional name for the instance. Attributes store data; methods are functions defined inside the class. class Account:  def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):  self.owner = owner  self.balance = balance  def deposit(self, amount):  self.balance += amount Inheritance lets a subclass reuse a parent class: class Savings(Account). The subclass can override methods and call the parent version through super(). Polymorphism means different classes can provide the same method name, so code can call obj.describe() without knowing the exact class. Encapsulation is the idea of keeping internal state controlled. S6.title: Python Glossary Overloaded Terms
S6.text: class: in Python a class is a blueprint for creating objects. It is not a category label as in classification problems. function: a reusable block of code defined with def. It is not necessarily a mathematical function. mode: when opening a file the mode string such as "r", "w" or "a" says how the file is used. statistics.mode(data) is a different thing: it returns the most frequent value. sample: random.sample(population, k) draws k unique elements without replacement. It has nothing to do with a statistical sample unless you use it to build one. normal: random.gauss(mu, sigma) and random.normalvariate(mu, sigma) draw numbers from a normal distribution. seed: random.seed(n) makes the random sequence reproducible, so a program prints the same random numbers on every run. iterable: an object you can loop over, such as a list or string.

S7.title: Python Reference Notes
S7.text:
COMMON ERRORS AND THEIR MEANING
SyntaxError: the code is not valid Python, for example a missing colon after if.
IndentationError: the indentation of a block is inconsistent.
NameError: a variable or function name was used before it was defined.
TypeError: an operation was applied to the wrong type, such as "a" + 1.
ValueError: the type is right but the value is not, such as int("abc").
KeyError: a dictionary key does not exist.
IndexError: a list index is outside the valid range.
ZeroDivisionError: division or modulo by zero.
FileNotFoundError: the file path does not exist.
